newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac election appeal underwhelms French left.
newsitem.headline: Chirac election appeal underwhelms French left.

text.p: Left-wing leaders on Wednesday brushed off French President Jacques Chirac's first public attempt, during a tight parliamentary election race, to convince voters to keep his centre-right coalition in power.

"How can you be believed when you don't tell the truth? How can you regain confidence when you are not credible?" opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin asked at a rally in Poitiers, western France.
"How can you have a 'new elan' when you didn't have an elan to begin with?" Jospin said, poking fun at Chirac's campaign plea for a new "shared elan" in France.
Chirac waded into the campaign for the May 25-June 1 election with a forceful assault on the left-wing opposition and an appeal for voters' trust and support.

"I need your support to continue the work we have begun together and which can only bear fruit over time. Let's seize our opportunity in a shared elan," he said in an article in 14 regional newspapers on the second anniversary of his election.
Left-wing politicians said Chirac had offered no new ideas, and many newspapers groused that they had been denied the honour of publishing his opinion column entitled "A Shared Elan".
Socialist European affairs expert Elisabeth Guigou said the president's "elan has fallen as flat as badly cooked souffle".
Communist party leader Robert Hue said voters should seize the chance to withdraw their confidence from Chirac, whose motto he said should be "we're on the wrong track, let's keep going".

Defending his unpopular record, Chirac said his government had had to "wipe the slate clean" after years of Socialist misrule, and urged the French people to move forward and not turn their backs on the course of history in the election.

Latest opinion polls show the combined left level or just ahead of the centre-right in voting intentions, but the ruling coalition is still projected to win a majority in seats because of the two-round voting system in single-member constituencies.
Accusing the Socialists without naming them of wasteful tax-and-spend policies, Chirac urged voters to give him the "political stability indispensible for effective action".
But Jospin said it was "surreal" that Chirac sought to blame the left for France's ills when the conservatives had been in power for four years.

In a potentially damaging revelation, former French head of state Valery Giscard d'Estaing disclosed that he had privately advised Chirac against dissolving parliament, urging him instead to do a better job of governing France.

In an unusually blunt interview on France 2 television, the centrist Giscard d'Estaing, who was president from 1974 until 1981, also hinted that Chirac should not reappoint Prime Minister Alain Juppe should the centre-right remain in power.
"He asked my opinion (on dissolving parliament) and I advised him against it," Giscard d'Estaing said.

"I told him, in effect, that he was taking a big risk since the debate would soon focus on the way in which France was being governed (and) that most of the French people were unhappy with the way in which they were being governed," he said.
"Under these conditions, it would have been more logical to first try to change the way they were governed."
With that decision now behind him, Chirac's message to voters should be that the centre-right would shift directions and pursue simpler and bolder policies, Giscard d'Estaing said.

Asked whether Juppe should be reappointed if the centre-right wins, Giscard d'Estaing urged the president to "listen to what the French people have wanted to tell you" and added that the next prime minister should come from "the new generation".
